* The [`Image`] widget has a fixed size in rows/columns. If the image pixel size exceeds the
 pixel area of the rows/columns, the image is scaled down proportionally to "fit" once, at the
 creation time of the [`Protocol`].

 and thus can never block the rendering thread/task. A lot of ratatui apps only use stateless
 widgets, so this factor is also important when chosing.

* The [StatefulImage] widget adapts to its render area at render-time. It can be set to fit,
 crop, or scale to the available render area.

 mutable state parameter.
 The resizing and encoding is blocking, and since it happens at render-time, it should always
 be offloaded to another thread or async task, to keep the UI responsive (see

# Plan: Ratatui (TUI) renderer — `pathland-render-tui`

## Feasibility assessment

Ratatui is **immediate-mode** (every terminal frame redraws the whole UI from the retained tree) — a great fit for Pathland's contract: the renderer stays a pure function of the opcode stream and only retains its **rendered-output tree + per-frame geometry cache** (id → Rect) for hit-testing and scroll/focus/cursor state. The transport is a natural fit: implement the existing `Pump` trait (`pathland-render-gtk/src/lib.rs:56-61`), reuse the canonical `RenderTree::apply_frame` decoder, and write inputs back through `Host::send_event` (renderer writes + wakes; **app** drains — same rule as GTK, `pathland-render-gtk/src/lib.rs:49-56`).

### Component → TUI mapping

| Component | Ratatui mapping | Feasibility |
|---|---|---|
| `TEXT` | `Paragraph`/`Line`/`Span` — wrap, `LINE_LIMIT` clamp, `TEXT_ALIGNMENT`, colors, weight/italic/underline/strike | ✅ native |
| `VSTACK`/`HSTACK`/`LAZY_*` | `Layout` (Vertical/Horizontal) + `Constraint`s from sizes/`SPACING`; eager lazy (spec-permitted) | ✅ native |
| `GRID`/`LAZY_VGRID`/`LAZY_HGRID`/`GRID_ROW` | nested `Layout` split; `GRID_TRACKS` flex/fixed/adaptive → `Constraint::{Fill,Length,Min}`; per-cell 2D placement; no-count → single-track (GTK parity) | ✅ native |
| `ZSTACK` | overlay draws (later = on top), 2D `ALIGNMENT` via per-child cell placement | ✅ native |
| `SCROLLVIEW` | clip child to viewport + `Scrollbar`; retained scroll offset → `SCROLL`/`WHEEL` events | ✅ native |
| `BUTTON` | styled block/paragraph; hover/press via mouse; Enter/Space; `POINTER_UP` on release | ✅ native |
| `SPACER`/`DIVIDER`/`COLOR` | flexible `Constraint` / `─` line / bg-fill area (`Fill` widget) | ✅ native |
| `PROGRESS_VIEW` | `Gauge` (determinate) / animated char spinner (indeterminate) | ✅ native |
| `GAUGE` | `Gauge`/`LineGauge` with min/max | ✅ native |
| `SLIDER` | `LineGauge` + thumb char; arrows/drag → `VALUE_CHANGED` | ✅ native |
| `TOGGLE`/`STEPPER` | `[x]`/switch text; `− value +`; click/keys → `VALUE_CHANGED` | ✅ native |
| `TEXT_FIELD`/`TEXT_EDITOR` | `Paragraph` + cursor; typing → `TEXT_CHANGED`; focus → `FOCUS_CHANGED`; Enter → `SUBMIT` | ✅ native |
| `PICKER`/`MENU` | `List` selectable / popup overlay `List` | ✅ native |
| `DATE_PICKER` | `calendar::Monthly` widget → `DATE_CHANGED` | ✅ native |
| `SHAPE` | `Canvas`/block chars (rect/circle/capsule approximation) | ⚠️ approximation |
| `IMAGE` | `ratatui-image` (Sixel/Kitty/iTerm2 + halfblock fallback) | ⚠️ feature-gated, terminal-dependent |
| `COLOR_PICKER` | swatch + hex edit | ⚠️ deferred |
| `AUDIO`/`VIDEO` | status line only (no terminal media) | ❌ out of scope |

### Property handling
Colors → Ratatui `Color` (16/256/truecolor); `FONT_WEIGHT`→Bold, `FONT_STYLE`→italic, `UNDERLINE`/`STRIKETHROUGH`→line styles; `FONT_SIZE`/`BORDER_RADIUS`/`SHADOW_*`/`BLUR`/`ROTATION`/`SCALE`/`OPACITY` → ignored (renderer fidelity choice, like other renderers); `VISIBLE` → skip draw; `CLIPS_TO_BUFFERS` → natural; `PADDING`/`CONTENT_MARGINS` → area insets; `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT` `FILL`/`HUG` → `Constraint`; `ALIGNMENT` 2D → cell placement (reuse `align_h`/`align_v`, `effective_fill`, `grid_cells` from `pathland-render-gtk/src/layout.rs` — all display-free, pure decisions). Design tokens: reuse `pathland_core::tokens::resolve` + a per-renderer default table + `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides.

## Architecture

**New crate** `lib/rust/crates/pathland-render-tui/` (workspace member, **rlib only** — a TUI is a Rust-only surface, no cdylib/JNA), deps: `pathland-core`, `pathland-core-transport`, `ratatui 0.30` (+ crossterm 0.29 backend, default). Modules:
- `host.rs` — the retained `RenderTree`/`HostNode` decoder + token resolution (see decision below).
- `layout.rs` — TUI layout: stack/grid/zstack rects, alignment, fill/hug → `Layout`+`Constraint` (mirrors GTK `layout.rs`, headless-testable).
- `draw.rs` — recursive widget pass over the tree → ratatui widgets into the `Frame`'s areas; keeps `HashMap<u32, Rect>` per frame for hit-testing.
- `input.rs` — crossterm event → protocol `Event` (`POINTER_*`, `KEY_*`, `WHEEL`, `VALUE_CHANGED`, `TEXT_CHANGED`, …), gated by `EVENT_LISTENERS`/`BINDING_ID`; key-code table (ASCII + special-key constants, documented in `spec/EVENTS.md`).
- `run.rs` — event loop: `next_frame()` → apply → `terminal.draw(draw)`; on input `send_input` + wake; the host (app) drains. `Pump` impls over `RingTransport` (mirrors `pump_once`).
- Demo `pathland-render-tui-demo` mirroring `pathland-render-gtk-demo`: DSL → `Engine` → ring → renderer → crossterm loop → drain → app state → re-emit.
- `status.md` per AGENTS.md; headless tests via Ratatui's **`TestBackend`**.

## Milestones (each ends green + committed)

- **M0 — Scaffold**: crate + workspace entry + `status.md`; shared decoder decision; `cargo build`/`test` green.
- **M1 — Static rendering**: stacks, `TEXT`, `SPACER`/`DIVIDER`/`COLOR`, `BUTTON` visual, `PROGRESS_VIEW`/`GAUGE`; spacing/padding/alignment/FILL; `TestBackend` golden tests; static demo renders a counter.
- **M2 — Interaction**: mouse hit-testing, keyboard + focus model, event write/wake + app drain; `BUTTON` click, `TOGGLE`/`SLIDER`/`STEPPER` value changes, `TEXT_FIELD` input; interactive demo.
- **M3 — Layout depth**: `GRID`/`GRID_ROW`/`GRID_TRACKS`, `ZSTACK` overlay, `SCROLLVIEW`+`Scrollbar`+`SCROLL`/`WHEEL`, `PICKER`/`MENU`/`DATE_PICKER`, `SHAPE` canvas.
- **M4 — Tokens + resize + polish**: token tables (light/dark) + overrides, terminal resize → `META::ENVIRONMENT` (app-side emit on SIGWINCH), key-code spec note, conformance/golden buffers, docs.
- **M5 (optional)** — `IMAGE` via `ratatui-image` behind a feature; media status line.

## Key risks / non-negotiables
- Terminal is cell-based: no pixels, no effects, images only via graphics protocols.
- Hit-testing depends on a fresh id→Rect map each frame — must be rebuilt in the same pass as drawing.
- The `no_std`/wasm32 guard is unaffected (renderer is std; core untouched).
- Renderer statelessness (AGENTS.md Principle 1): only output-tree + geometry + input-focus/scroll cursor retained; scroll/cursor are rendered-output state, app owns all logic.

141:     /// Re-resolve every `DESIGN_TOKEN`-typed property against the theme, the
142:     /// active scheme, and the parent-fallback chain, materializing concrete
143:     /// values into [`HostNode::properties`] (numeric) or [`HostNode::strings`]
144:     /// (STRING tokens). The paths are kept in [`HostNode::token_refs`] for
145:     /// re-resolution on scheme change.
146:     pub fn resolve_tokens(&mut self) {
147:         let tables = TokenTables {
148:             overrides: &self.overrides,
149:             dark_overrides: &self.dark_overrides,
150:             defaults: &self.defaults,
151:             dark_defaults: &self.dark_defaults,
152:         };
153:         for node in self.nodes.values_mut() {
154:             let refs: Vec<(u16, String)> = node.token_refs.iter().map(|(k, v)| (*k, v.clone())).collect();
155:             for (prop, path) in refs {
156:                 if let Some(value) = resolve_token(&path, self.scheme, &tables) {
157:                     match value {
158:                         TokenValue::Str(s) => {
159:                             node.strings.insert(prop, s);
160:                         }
161:                         _ => {
162:                             if let Some(bits) = value.to_bits() {
163:                                 node.properties.insert(prop, bits);
164:                             }
165:                         }
166:                     }
167:                 }
168:             }
169:         }
170:     }

172:     /// Apply a frame's opcodes to this tree (a delta).
173:     pub fn apply_frame(&mut self, frame: &Frame<'_>) {
174:         for op in frame.opcodes() {
175:             match (op.category(), op.command()) {
176:                 (category::TREE, tree::CREATE_NODE) => {
177:                     let id = op.a();
178:                     let ty = op.b() as u16;
179:                     let entry = self.nodes.entry(id).or_default();
180:                     entry.id = id;
181:                     entry.component_type = ty;
182:                 }
183:                 (category::TREE, tree::DELETE_NODE) => {
184:                     self.nodes.remove(&op.a());
185:                 }
186:                 (category::TREE, tree::INSERT_CHILD) => {
187:                     let (parent, child) = (op.a(), op.b());
188:                     if let Some(p) = self.nodes.get_mut(&parent) {
189:                         if !p.children.contains(&child) {
190:                             p.children.push(child);
191:                         }
192:                     }
193:                     if let Some(c) = self.nodes.get_mut(&child) {
194:                         c.parent = Some(parent);
195:                     }
196:                 }
197:                 (category::TREE, tree::REMOVE_CHILD) => {
198:                     let (parent, child) = (op.a(), op.b());
199:                     if let Some(p) = self.nodes.get_mut(&parent) {
200:                         p.children.retain(|c| *c != child);
201:                     }
202:                     if let Some(c) = self.nodes.get_mut(&child) {
203:                         c.parent = None;
204:                     }
205:                 }
206:                 (category::TREE, tree::MOVE_CHILD) => {
207:                     let (parent, child, new_index) = (op.a(), op.b(), op.c() as usize);
208:                     if let Some(p) = self.nodes.get_mut(&parent) {
209:                         if let Some(pos) = p.children.iter().position(|c| *c == child) {
210:                             p.children.remove(pos);
211:                         }
212:                         let idx = if new_index == usize::MAX {
213:                             p.children.len()
214:                         } else {
215:                             new_index.min(p.children.len())
216:                         };
217:                         p.children.insert(idx, child);
218:                     }
219:                 }
220:                 (category::PARAMETER, parameter::SET_PROPERTY) => {
221:                     let prop_id = op.b() as u16;
222:                     let vt = (op.b() >> 16) as u8;
223:                     if let Some(n) = self.nodes.get_mut(&op.a()) {
224:                         if vt == value_type::STRING {
225:                             // Resolve the arena offset into the actual text.
226:                             if let Ok(text) = frame.arena_str(op.c()) {
227:                                 n.strings.insert(prop_id, text.to_string());
228:                             }
229:                         } else if vt == value_type::DESIGN_TOKEN {
230:                             // A token reference: keep the path for resolution
231:                             // against the theme (spec/TOKENS.md). C is the arena
232:                             // offset of the token path.
233:                             if let Ok(path) = frame.arena_str(op.c()) {
234:                                 n.token_refs.insert(prop_id, path.to_string());
235:                             }
236:                         } else {
237:                             n.properties.insert(prop_id, op.c());
238:                         }
239:                     }
240:                 }
241:                 (category::PARAMETER, parameter::SET_TEXT) => {
242:                     if let Some(n) = self.nodes.get_mut(&op.a()) {
243:                         n.text = frame.arena_str(op.b()).ok().map(|s| s.to_string());
244:                     }
245:                 }
246:                 (category::PARAMETER, parameter::SET_DESIGN_TOKEN) => {
247:                     // Global override: A = arenaRef (token path), B = valueType,
248:                     // C = value (for STRING, an arenaRef to the value string).
249:                     if let Ok(path) = frame.arena_str(op.a()) {
250:                         let vt = (op.b() & 0xFF) as u8;
251:                         let value = if vt == value_type::STRING {
252:                             frame
253:                                 .arena_str(op.c())
254:                                 .map(|s| TokenValue::Str(s.to_string()))
255:                                 .unwrap_or(TokenValue::U32(0))
256:                         } else {
257:                             TokenValue::from_wire(vt, op.c()).unwrap_or(TokenValue::U32(op.c()))
258:                         };
259:                         if let Some(bare) = path.strip_prefix("dark.") {
260:                             self.dark_overrides.insert(bare.to_string(), value);
261:                         } else {
262:                             self.overrides.insert(path.to_string(), value);
263:                         }
264:                     }
265:                 }
266:                 _ => {}
267:             }
268:         }
269:         self.resolve_tokens();
270:     }

21:     ("theme_bg_color", "color.background"),

37:     let dark = settings.is_gtk_application_prefer_dark_theme()
38:         || settings
39:             .gtk_theme_name()
40:             .as_deref()
41:             .map_or(false, |name| name.ends_with("-dark"));

```rust
use pathland_core::{component_type, property_id, size};
use pathland_host::{HostNode, RenderTree};
use ratatui::layout::{Constraint, Direction, Layout, Rect};

pub const FILL: f32 = -1.0;
pub const HUG_CONTENT: f32 = -2.0;

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
pub struct Edges {
    pub top: u16,
    pub right: u16,
    pub bottom: u16,
    pub left: u16,
}

impl Edges {
    pub const ZERO: Edges = Edges { top: 0, right: 0, bottom: 0, left: 0 };
    pub fn horizontal(&self) -> u16 { self.left + self.right }
    pub fn vertical(&self) -> u16 { self.top + self.bottom }
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
pub struct Size { pub width: u16, pub height: u16 }

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
pub enum CrossPos { Start, Center, End }

pub fn f32_prop(node: &HostNode, prop: u16) -> Option<f32> {
    node.properties.get(&prop).copied().map(f32::from_bits)
}

fn fixed(node: &HostNode, prop: u16) -> Option<u16> {
    match f32_prop(node, prop) {
        Some(v) if v > 0.0 => Some(v.round() as u16),
        _ => None,
    }
}

fn fills(node: &HostNode, prop: u16) -> bool {
    matches!(f32_prop(node, prop), Some(v) if v == size::FILL)
}

pub fn padding_edges(node: &HostNode) -> Edges {
    let uniform = f32_prop(node, property_id::PADDING).unwrap_or(0.0).round().max(0.0) as u16;
    let top = f32_prop(node, property_id::PADDING_TOP).unwrap_or(uniform as f32).round().max(0.0) as u16;
    ...

    let cm = f32_prop(node, property_id::CONTENT_MARGINS).unwrap_or(0.0).round().max(0.0) as u16;

    ...
}
```

```rust
fn stack_natural(node, tree, vertical) -> Size {
    let e = padding_edges(node);
    let sp = spacing(node);
    let children = &node.children;
    let mut main_total = 0u16;
    let mut cross_max = 0u16;
    let mut n = 0;

        if vertical { main_total += s.height; cross_max = cross_max.max(s.width); }

    if vertical { Size{ width: cross_max + e.horizontal(), height: main_total + gaps + e.vertical() } }

}
```

```rust
fn place_stack(tree, node, area, dir, out) {
    let e = padding_edges(node);
    let inner = inset(area, &e);
    let sp = spacing(node);
    let children = node.children.clone();
    if children.is_empty() { return; }

    // classify
    let mut sizes: Vec<u16> = Vec::with_capacity(children.len());
    let mut flexible: Vec<bool> = Vec::with_capacity(children.len());
    let mut fixed_total = 0u16;
    let mut flexible_count = 0u16;
    for cid in &children {
        let cn = tree.node(*cid);
        let natural = natural_size(tree, *cid);
        let main = main_size(natural, dir);
        let fills_main = cn.map_or(false, |n| fills_on_main(n, dir));
        if fills_main { flexible.push(true); flexible_count += 1; sizes.push(0); }
        else { flexible.push(false); fixed_total += main.max(1); sizes.push(main.max(1)); }
    }
    let avail = main_len(inner, dir);
    let gaps = sp.saturating_mul(children.len().saturating_sub(1) as u16);
    let leftover = avail.saturating_sub(fixed_total + gaps);
    let per_flex = if flexible_count > 0 { leftover / flexible_count } else { 0 };

    // build constraints with spacing
    let mut constraints = Vec::with_capacity(children.len() * 2 - 1);
    for (i, (s, flex)) in sizes.iter().zip(&flexible).enumerate() {
        if i > 0 { constraints.push(Constraint::Length(sp)); }
        constraints.push(if *flex { Constraint::Fill(1) } else { Constraint::Length(*s) });
    }
    // Note: per_flex unused since Fill distributes leftover automatically. Keep Fill(1).

    let cells = Layout::default().direction(dir).constraints(constraints).split(inner);
    for (cid, cell) in children.iter().zip(cells.iter()) {
        let Some(cn) = tree.node(*cid) else { continue };
        let child_area = align_cross(*cell, tree, *cid, cn, dir, node);
        place(tree, *cid, child_area, out);
    }
}
```

```rust
    let cross_axis_fill = match dir {
        Direction::Vertical => fills(cn, property_id::WIDTH),
```

input.content:
# pathland-render-tui — implementation status

**Last updated:** October 2, 2026

The **Ratatui (TUI) renderer**: maps opcode frames incrementally onto native
terminal widgets (immediate-mode redraw each terminal frame). Protocol contract:
`spec/`. Retained-tree decoding + token resolution come from the shared
`pathland-host` crate.

## Implemented

- **Components → widgets** (`render.rs`):
  - `VSTACK`/`HSTACK`/`LAZY_VSTACK`/`LAZY_HSTACK` → ratatui `Layout` (spacing/
    padding/`ALIGNMENT` cross-axis, `FILL`/greedy children split leftover on the
    main axis),
  - `TEXT` → `Paragraph` (per-line `Span`s; `COLOR`/`BACKGROUND_COLOR`/
    `FONT_WEIGHT`/`FONT_STYLE`/`UNDERLINE`/`STRIKETHROUGH` styles; `TEXT_ALIGNMENT`;
    `LINE_LIMIT` truncation),
  - `BUTTON` → `Paragraph` + `Block` border (`BORDER_WIDTH`/`BORDER_COLOR`);
    composite bodies render as a horizontal row,
  - `SPACER` → flexible `Constraint`; `DIVIDER` → `─` line; `COLOR` → `Fill`
    background,
  - `PROGRESS_VIEW` → `Gauge` (determinate) / animated braille spinner
    (indeterminate), `GAUGE` → `LineGauge` (`VALUE`/`MIN_VALUE`/`MAX_VALUE`).
- **Layout** (`layout.rs`, pure + headless-testable): bottom-up natural cell
  size, top-down `Rect` assignment; per-edge `PADDING` (`PADDING_*` > `PADDING`
  > `CONTENT_MARGINS`), `SPACING` gaps, 2D `ALIGNMENT` → cross-axis position
  (`align_h`/`align_v`, codes 0–8), `FILL`/`HUG`/Fixed `WIDTH`/`HEIGHT`, greedy
  primitives (`SPACER`/`COLOR`/`SCROLLVIEW`). 1 protocol point = 1 cell.
- **Per-frame geometry cache**: `id → Rect` (`TuiRenderer::rect`) for
  hit-testing; rebuilt every draw.
- **Retained-tree decoding** via `pathland_host::RenderTree` (`apply_frame`),
  incl. `SET_DESIGN_TOKEN` overrides + token refs; `TuiRenderer::set_scheme`
  re-resolves on scheme change.
- **Demo** (`pathland-render-tui-demo`): DSL → `Engine` → shared ring →
  renderer; quits on `q`/`Esc`/`Ctrl+C`.

## Not implemented / gaps

- **No input yet** (M2 planned): mouse hit-testing → `POINTER_*`, keyboard →
  `KEY_*`, `VALUE_CHANGED`/`TEXT_CHANGED` from controls, `EVENT_LISTENERS`/
  `BINDING_ID` gating, event write + wake/drain loop.
- **No grid/ZStack/ScrollView yet** (M3 planned): `GRID`/`GRID_ROW`/
  `GRID_TRACKS`, `ZSTACK` overlay + 2D alignment, `SCROLLVIEW` + `Scrollbar` +
  `SCROLL`/`WHEEL`, `PICKER`/`MENU`/`DATE_PICKER`, `SHAPE`.
- **No design-token default tables for TUI colors** yet (`SET_DESIGN_TOKEN`
  overrides decode, but `COLOR`-token refs resolve to the shared `pathland-host`
  concrete defaults; a TUI-specific table + scheme detection is a follow-up).
- **No terminal-resize reporting** (`META::ENVIRONMENT` viewport) — the app
  re-draws to `frame.area()` automatically, but the guest is not notified.
- **`IMAGE`** deferred (feature-gated `ratatui-image`, M5); **`AUDIO`/`VIDEO`**
  out of scope (status line only); effects (`SHADOW_*`/`BLUR`/`ROTATION`/
  `SCALE`/`OPACITY`) and `FONT_SIZE`/`BORDER_RADIUS` ignored (renderer fidelity).

## Verified by

`cargo test -p pathland-render-tui` — layout decisions (stack placement,
spacing gaps, filler absorption, `FILL` stretch, cross-axis alignment, padding)
and `TestBackend` buffer assertions (text, spacing, button border, fill color,
gauge ratio). `cargo run -p pathland-render-tui-demo` for a visual check.

```rust
pub fn run<P: FrameSource + DriverTransport>(pump: &mut P, mut wake: impl FnMut()) {
    let mut renderer = TuiRenderer::new();
    // apply initial frames
    drain_frames(pump, &mut renderer);
    enable_raw_mode + alternate screen;
    let mut quit = false;
    while !quit {
        // apply any new frames
        drain_frames(pump, &mut renderer);
        terminal.draw(|f| renderer.draw(f, f.area()))...;
        // handle input
        if poll(timeout) {
            match read() {
                Key(q/Esc/Ctrl-C) => quit,
                Mouse/Move/Scroll => { for ev in renderer.handle_input(&input) { pump.send_input(&ev); } wake(); }
                Resize => {}
            }
        }
        renderer.tick();
    }
    restore;
}
```

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run the Java + Ratatui (TUI) desktop demo: the shared MusicPlayerView under
# the native TUI renderer, over the libpathland_core shared ring.
#
# Quit with q or Ctrl+C. No window/display needed — run inside any terminal.
set -euo pipefail
source "$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)/lib.sh"

# Build the Rust dylibs the demo links: the core ring (libpathland_core) and
# the TUI renderer (libpathland_render_tui).
(cd "$ROOT/lib/rust" && cargo build -p pathland-core-capi -p pathland-render-tui)
java_install

case "$(uname -s)" in
  Darwin)  EXT=".dylib" ;;
  Linux)   EXT=".so" ;;
  MINGW*|MSYS*|CYGWIN*) EXT=".dll" ;;
  *) echo "unsupported OS: $(uname -s)" >&2; exit 1 ;;
esac

cd "$ROOT/lib/java/pathland-tui-demo"

CPFILE="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$CPFILE"' EXIT
mvn -q dependency:build-classpath -Dmdep.outputFile="$CPFILE"
CP="target/classes:$(cat "$CPFILE")"

exec java \
  -Dpathland.core.lib="$ROOT/lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_core$EXT" \
  -Dpathland.tui.lib="$ROOT/lib/rust/target/debug/libpathland_render_tui$EXT" \
  -cp "$CP" com.pathland.demo.tui.TuiHost

parts.text: Branch `fix/seekbar-issue` created from `main` (clean). What's the seekbar issue you want to fix?

The issue I have is related to event handling / change detection in general. When sliding a progressbar (fx. seekbar) it will emit events about it value. It will then update the value on the server which emits the change to the ui. But because the user i still sliding the value does no longer match the current position. The result is a flickering progress bar.

The user describes a classic echo-loop / control-echo problem: while dragging a slider (seekbar), the app emits VALUE_CHANGED; the app updates its signal, re-emits SET_PROPERTY VALUE back; the renderer applies the value back to the control while the user is still dragging — causing flickering because the user's finger position and the echoed value conflict.

This is a well-known problem in the GTK renderer too — the AGENTS.md and status.md mentioned "Re-entrant control signals" and "control-echo loop" handling:
- render-gtk status.md: "Re-entrant control signals: applying a frame borrows the pump... a programmatic value change fires the connected GTK signal synchronously and re-entered emit, double-borrowing the pump and panicking. Such events are now deferred to the idle pump (flush_pending before each frame), which also prevents a control-echo loop when the host writes the same value back."

So GTK handles the echo at the signal level (deferring). But the flicker issue is different: it's about the visual state during an active drag. The renderer sets the slider's position from VALUE (from the app's echo), overriding the user's current drag position → flicker.

The user says "event handling / change detection in general". They want to understand and fix this: when the user is actively sliding, the renderer should not re-apply echoed VALUE updates to the control's visual position (it should keep showing the user's drag position), and possibly should not re-emit events for changes that originated from itself (echo suppression).

Let me research the current state of the codebase to ground the plan:
1. GTK renderer: how SLIDER is updated (`update` → control events, `GtkScale::set_value`), the `BINDING_ID` gating, the `attach_control_events` for slider → `ValueChanged` on `value_changed` signal, and the echo suppression (there might be a flag). Let me look at the GTK slider handling.
2. TUI renderer: slider → LineGauge ratio from VALUE; arrow adjust → VALUE_CHANGED. The same echo problem would apply in the TUI.
3. HTML/TS DOM renderer: the slider input → VALUE_CHANGED; applying SET_PROPERTY VALUE back to the input while dragging → flicker. The TS client (`apply.ts`) — does it have echo suppression? The `Na` / `Ze` functions apply VALUE to input[type=range]. Let me check if there's suppression while the input is being dragged.
4. The Java DSL emitter / InputDispatcher: how VALUE_CHANGED flows into the bound signal, and how the signal re-emits SET_PROPERTY VALUE. Is there equality suppression on the signal side (Signals.set with equality)? If the value is equal, no re-emit — that would prevent the echo for identical values. But during a drag, the user's value differs from the echoed one, so it re-emits, causing the flicker.

The core design question: how to prevent the renderer from echoing back the user's own input, and how to avoid flicker when the app's authoritative value (from server) lags/conflicts with the in-progress drag.

Standard solutions:
1. **Local echo suppression / "in-flight" drag state**: While a drag is in progress on a control, the renderer treats the control as "user-driven" and does not apply VALUE updates from the app to the control's visual position (the drag position is authoritative until release). On release, the final value is emitted and subsequent app updates apply. This is the "value-in-flight" pattern. The renderer retains transient input state (allowed: it's rendered-output/input state, not app business state — like the scroll offset/focus).

2. **Echo suppression by origin**: Don't re-emit events that originated from the renderer (already partly done in GTK: the `emit` closure defers re-entrant signals; but the re-emitted SET_PROPERTY from the app causes set_value which fires value_changed again → the renderer sends VALUE_CHANGED again → loop).    Structural properties (`MIN_VALUE`/`MAX_VALUE`/`STEP_VALUE`, size, style)
   still apply.
2. **Do not re-report events for skipped writes.** Because the write was not
   applied, no change signal fires and no `VALUE_CHANGED` is re-emitted — the
   echo loop is broken at the source.
3. **Resume on session end.** When the interaction ends (release / blur), the
   in-flight state clears and inbound updates apply again; the final position
   was already reported by the interaction's own events.

This is **renderer state, not application state** (AGENTS.md Principle 1): the
in-edit value is transient input/rendered-output state, like the scroll offset
and the text caret.

The session boundaries are also **reported as events** so the application can
suppress echoes of *derived* state the renderer cannot know about (a custom
drag offset, a drawn position):

- `FOCUS_CHANGED` (0x08) — the control gained/lost focus.
- `EDITING_CHANGED` (0x09) — a value/text edit session started/ended.

Both are reported **only when the target declared the matching `EVENT_LISTENERS`
bit** (`FOCUS` = `1<<5`, `EDITING` = `1<<6`). An application that observes
`EDITING_CHANGED { editing: true }` should hold back authoritative echoes of the
edited state until `{ editing: false }`.

The mechanism is **per-state / per-session**: implemented today for value drags
(`SLIDER`); text editing and other continuous inputs use the same path.

1. **Single actor thread**: `PathlandRegistry` serializes ALL session work on a single daemon executor thread (`pathland-actor`). `dispatch`, `environment`, `resync`, `close` all `actor.execute(...)`. The send path (`endFrame → send → conn.send`) runs ON this actor thread.

2. **`dispatch` catches exceptions at the session level** (`PathlandSession.dispatch` wraps `inputDispatcher.dispatch` in try/catch and logs "dropping event batch"). BUT — the `send()` path is inside `endFrame()`, which is called during `emitter` operations triggered by `inputDispatcher.dispatch` → `signal.set` → effect → `emitter` emit → `sink.endFrame` → `send`. If `send` throws (outside the try? no — `FrameCodec.encodeFrame` is OUTSIDE the try, `conn.send` inside), then:
   - `conn.send(bytes)` throws → caught → `connection = null` (returns normally).
   - `FrameCodec.encodeFrame(frame)` throws → NOT caught → propagates up through endFrame → emitter → signal effect → inputDispatcher.dispatch → PathlandSession.dispatch try/catch → caught → "dropping event batch" logged. So the actor thread survives (the exception is caught at the dispatch level). BUT the connection is NOT nulled in this case (the exception was before conn.send). And the batch is dropped.

3. **The actor thread could die** if an exception escapes `actor.execute`'s Runnable — but the session's dispatch catches RuntimeException, and `session()`/`applyEnvironment`/`resync` are not wrapped. If `resync` or `applyEnvironment` throws, the Runnable on the actor thread throws → the ExecutorService task fails → the single-thread executor keeps going (a failed task doesn't kill the executor; the next task still runs). So a one-off throw doesn't stop the actor.

So reconnect works and re-syncs.

Confirmed: the Java `FrameOpcodeSink` accumulates a frame per `beginFrame/endFrame` pair, and `PathlandSession` overrides `endFrame` to `send(frame)` immediately. So **each signal change produces one tiny WS frame sent immediately** — no coalescing/batching on the Java server side. During a drag (dozens of VALUE_CHANGED/sec), that's dozens of tiny WS messages/sec. On a remote host with a slow client, this burst can overflow Quarkus's send queue → `sendBinary` failures → **swallowed** → the server silently stops delivering while the WS stays open.

I now have a coherent, code-grounded diagnosis:

**Root cause**: 
- `QuarkusConnection.send` (`QuarkusConnection.java:16-18`) swallows every send failure (`failure -> {}`), so `PathlandSession.send` can never detect that deliveries stopped.
- `PathlandSession.send` only clears the connection when `conn.send` *throws* or `!conn.isOpen()` — neither happens with the swallow (and Quarkus's send path failing doesn't mark the connection closed).
- The Java server sends **one WS frame per signal change, unbuffered** (`PathlandSession` overrides `FrameOpcodeSink.endFrame` → `send(frame)` immediately). A seekbar drag produces a burst of tiny frames; over a remote/slow link the send queue overflows and `sendBinary` subscriptions fail — silently.
- Result: the browser's WS stays "open" but the server delivers nothing → permanent freeze, no reconnect (the DOM client only reconnects on close).

Contrast: `SpringConnection.send` throws on failure → `PathlandSession.send` nulls the connection → (Spring closes the session on send failure) → the client reconnects → RESYNC recovers. That's why the symptom is Quarkus-specific (the Docker/quarkus demo is the deployed one).

**Fix plan** (multi-part, ordered by impact):

1. **Quarkus adapter: surface failures** — on send failure, close the connection so the session detects it (`isOpen()` → false → `connection = null`) and the client reconnects+RESYNCs:
   ```java
   connection.sendBinary(bytes).subscribe().with(
       ignored -> {},
       failure -> { try { connection.close(); } catch (Exception ignored) {} });
   ```
   This converts silent-stall into recoverable reconnect. (Spring already behaves this way.)

2. **Serialize sends on the Quarkus adapter** — avoid concurrent `sendBinary` subscriptions racing (rapid sends from the actor thread). Chain sends so only one is in flight at a time (an `AtomicReference<Uni>`/queue pattern). Prevents transient drops and ordering issues.

3. **Coalesce Java-side deltas** (the highest-value structural fix): batch deltas like the Rust transport's `Batcher` (max_interval + max_batch_bytes) instead of sending one frame per signal change. Reduces the burst by orders of magnitude (a drag's intermediate values coalesce), so the send queue can't overflow. Implement a small `DeltaBatcher` in the session: accumulate frames from `endFrame`, flush on a timer (~16-30ms) or when bytes exceed a threshold. This also generally reduces WS churn (every web app benefits).

4. **Make `PathlandSession.send` defensive** — move `FrameCodec.encodeFrame` inside the try (it currently sits outside, so an encode exception propagates unhandled into the actor), and on any send failure, also `connection.close()` (best-effort) so the client reconnects deterministically. Minor hardening.

5. **Tests / verification**: 
   - Unit test the `QuarkusConnection` failure path is hard (Quarkus runtime); instead test the session's `send` recovery (a fake connection that fails → next `isOpen()` false → connection cleared) — but `PathlandConnection` is an interface; add a server-core test with a failing connection asserting `PathlandSession` stops sending / the session is resyncable.
   - Test the `DeltaBatcher` coalescing (N frames → ≤ M sends, latest-value-wins).
   - Manual: run the Quarkus demo remotely (or with a throttled client) and drag the seekbar; verify deltas keep flowing and that a forced send failure triggers a client reconnect+RESYNC.
   - `mvn test` across the reactor.

Now — I should also double check the DOM client reconnect behavior: on WS close it reconnects with backoff and sends RESYNC. Yes (from the bundle: `onclose → scheduleReconnect`; on open after reconnect `send(st())` for RESYNC). Good — so closing the WS on send failure yields recovery.

Let me reconsider "suddenly stop sending events... via the websocket" — could it be the SERVER-side `resync()`/`renderFull` on reconnect causing an exception that... no. Or the actor thread dying? Single-thread executor survives failed tasks. Or a memory issue (sink strings growing)? The FrameOpcodeSink resets per frame. OK.

Could the stop be caused by the in-flight FOCUS/EDITING events I added? Those are client-side TS (already existed) — the merge added GTK-only session events, not TS. So no new client events. And the merged TS in-flight suppression doesn't change client→server sends. So the merged PR didn't introduce this WS bug — it's pre-existing (the seekbar drag burst). Good to note clearly so the user knows this is a separate server bug, not a regression of the flicker fix.

## Root cause — Quarkus swallows send failures; Java sends unbuffered

**1. `QuarkusConnection.send` swallows every failure** (`QuarkusConnection.java:16-18`):
```java
connection.sendBinary(bytes).subscribe().with(ignored -> {}, failure -> {});
```
The `failure -> {}` discards errors. `PathlandSession.send` (`PathlandSession.java:131-143`) only clears the connection when `conn.send` **throws** or `!conn.isOpen()` — with the swallow, neither ever fires, so the session keeps "sending" into a broken path forever.

**2. The Java server sends one WS frame per signal change, unbuffered** (`PathlandSession` overrides `FrameOpcodeSink.endFrame` → `send(frame)` immediately; `FrameOpcodeSink.java:46`). A seekbar drag bursts dozens of tiny frames/sec; over a remote/slow link the Quarkus send queue overflows, `sendBinary` subscriptions fail — silently.

**Result:** the browser's WS stays "open" but the server delivers nothing → permanent freeze with **no reconnect** (the DOM client only reconnects on WS close).

**Why Quarkus but not Spring:** `SpringConnection.send` (`SpringConnection.java:17-23`) throws on failure → `PathlandSession.send` nulls the connection → Spring closes the session → the client reconnects → RESYNC recovers. The Quarkus Docker demo (docs/DEPLOY.md) is the one with the silent-stall.

## Fix plan (server-side, on a branch from main)

1. **`QuarkusConnection.send` — surface failures** (essential): on failure, close the connection (`connection.close()`), so the next `send` sees `!isOpen()` → the session clears it → the client's WS closes → it reconnects + requests RESYNC (the client already does this). Converts silent-stall into recoverable reconnect — matching Spring's behavior.
2. **Serialize sends on the Quarkus adapter**: chain `sendBinary` subscriptions (only one in flight) to avoid concurrent-subscription races during rapid deltas.
3. **Coalesce Java-side deltas** (structural, highest value): batch frames like the Rust transport's `Batcher` (flush on ~16–30 ms or a byte threshold, latest-value-wins) instead of one frame per signal change — cuts the drag burst by orders of magnitude so the queue can't overflow. Every web app benefits.
4. **Harden `PathlandSession.send`**: move `FrameCodec.encodeFrame` inside the try (it currently sits outside, so an encode exception escapes into the actor thread uncaught), and on any send failure also best-effort `connection.close()`.

**Verification:** a `PathlandSession` unit test with a failing `PathlandConnection` (send throws → connection cleared → recoverable); a `DeltaBatcher` coalescing test; `mvn test`; then a manual remote run — drag the seekbar and confirm deltas keep flowing and a forced send failure triggers client reconnect+RESYNC.

Now — a concern: `PathlandConnection` interface has only `send` and `isOpen`. My `closeConnection` checks `instanceof AutoCloseable` — the Quarkus/Spring adapters don't implement AutoCloseable currently. I could add `AutoCloseable` to QuarkusConnection so it closes on failure (though the Quarkus adapter already closes itself on send failure asynchronously; the session-level closeConnection is for the synchronous-throw case like Spring). Actually — for Quarkus, the failure is surfaced asynchronously (the adapter closes itself). For Spring, `send` throws → session catches → closeConnection (Spring doesn't implement AutoCloseable → no-op, but Spring closes the session itself on send failure). So closeConnection is a nice-to-have; fine as-is.

Now — a subtle issue with the batcher + `connection` guard in `endFrame`: I check `conn == null || !conn.isOpen()` in endFrame. But with the Quarkus async failure, `isOpen()` returns false only after the adapter's `failed` flag is set (which happens in the async failure callback). Between the failure and the callback, endFrame might append to the batcher → later flush → send (no-op, adapter drops). Fine.

Another subtlety: `endFrame` drops frames when `!conn.isOpen()`. But the batcher's flush (scheduler) may still send pending batches after the connection is dropped → `sendBatch` checks connection → drops. Fine.

Now — there's a REAL correctness concern with batching and the `endFrame` connectivity guard: **during a drag on a healthy connection, endFrame appends; the batcher flushes on the timer; sendBatch sends.** Good.

But wait — there's a subtle issue with **frame ordering and the mount/snapshot**: `renderFull` (resync) produces a big frame; endFrame appends it to the batcher; `resync` then calls `batcher.flush()`. If there were pending delta opcodes before the resync, the merged batch would contain the old deltas PLUS the snapshot — that's fine (they apply in order, snapshot last). Good.

Now — **the `FrameCodec` import**: still used in dispatch. Good.

Now — one more important consideration: **the batcher's scheduler thread and the `sendBatch` connection check.** `sendBatch` reads `connection` (volatile) and calls `conn.send(bytes)`. For Quarkus, `conn.send` (the adapter) queues + drains (async). Non-blocking. Good.

Now let me also check: `PathlandSession` still imports `Frame` (used in the endFrame `Frame frame = frame()`). Yes — `com.pathland.view.emit.Frame`. The `send(Frame)` method was removed but `Frame` is still used in endFrame. Good. `FrameCodec` still used. Good.

parts.text:
Done. The remote WebSocket silent-stop is fixed on `fix/ws-send-recovery`.

## What was wrong
The **Quarkus** WebSocket adapter swallowed every send failure (`failure -> {}`), so `PathlandSession` never learned deliveries stopped. Meanwhile the Java server sent **one tiny WS frame per signal change, unbuffered** — a seekbar drag bursts dozens of frames/sec, which overflows the send queue on a remote/slow link. Result: the browser's WS stayed "open" but the server delivered nothing, and the DOM client never reconnects (it only reconnects on close).

## What landed (all four)
1. **`QuarkusConnection`** — sends are now **serialized** (one `sendBinary` subscription in flight, rest queued), and a **send failure closes the connection** → the session drops it → the client's WS closes → it reconnects + requests `META::RESYNC`. Recoverable instead of silent-stall.
2. **`DeltaBatcher`** (new, `pathland-server-core`) — merges per-signal frames (opcodes + a single **rebased string section**) into one network batch, flushed ~20 ms or 16 KB — the Java analogue of the Rust `Batcher`. A drag burst collapses to ~50 messages/sec. Wired into `PathlandSession`'s `endFrame` (only for live, connected sessions).
3. **`PathlandSession.sendBatch`** — dropped connection on any send failure (+ best-effort close); `resync()` flushes immediately; `close()` shuts down the batcher.
4. **status.md** updates for `pathland-server-core` + the Quarkus starter.

## Verified
`mvn` reactor tests green — `PathlandSessionTest` 9 (incl. new *drops failed connection + recovers on reconnect*), `DeltaBatcherTest` 2 (rebased-string merge + 100-frame burst → 1 send). No Rust/TS changes.

## To try it
Rebuild the demo (`cargo build -p pathland-render-html` if needed, then `./scripts/run-quarkus-demo.sh`), host it remotely, drag the seekbar — deltas keep flowing, and a network break now recovers via reconnect+RESYNC instead of freezing.

2. `QuarkusConnection` — serialized sends + failure-surfacing. This is Quarkus-specific.
3. `PathlandSession.sendBatch` — drop connection on failure. Module-agnostic.

So the DeltaBatcher + sendBatch hardening are in `pathland-server-core` — shared by both starters. So Spring Boot **already gets the batching + send-failure-drop** from this change (they're in the shared session runtime).

What Spring does NOT get from my change:
- The serialized-send + failure-close behavior in `QuarkusConnection`. Spring has its own `SpringConnection`.

Let me analyze `SpringConnection.send`:
```java

    } catch (Exception e) {

}
```

Spring's `WebSocketSession.sendMessage` is **synchronous and blocking**. It throws on failure (which the session catches → drops connection). So:
- **Bursts**: With the DeltaBatcher, the burst is coalesced into ~50 messages/sec, so the send rate is already low. But Spring's `sendMessage` is called on the batcher's scheduler thread (a daemon thread) now — before my change it was called on the actor thread (from endFrame). Either way it's synchronous blocking. If the client is slow, `sendMessage` can block the scheduler thread. But since the batcher serializes/coalesces, the burst is controlled.
- **Failure handling**: Spring's `sendMessage` throws → `sendBatch` catches → connection nulled. So Spring already recovers (client reconnect + RESYNC). Good — that was the original analysis (Spring throws).

So the answer: **Yes, mostly** — Spring gets the DeltaBatcher (burst coalescing) + the send-failure-drop hardening automatically since both live in the shared `pathland-server-core`. What Spring does NOT get is the Quarkus-specific serialized-send queue, but Spring's `sendMessage` is inherently synchronous (serialized by the WebSocketSession internally — Spring requires that sendMessage calls be serialized; concurrent calls from multiple threads can throw `IllegalStateException`!). 

Wait — that's important. Spring's `WebSocketSession.sendMessage` is NOT thread-safe for concurrent sends. After my change, sends happen on the **DeltaBatcher's scheduler thread** (single thread per session — each PathlandSession has its own DeltaBatcher with its own scheduler thread). So sends for a given session are serialized on that one scheduler thread. Good — no concurrent sendMessage from the batcher. But before my change, sends happened on the actor thread (single thread). Both are single-threaded per session, so no concurrent sendMessage within a session. Across sessions, different connections → different sessions → fine.

But — is there a concurrency concern in Spring where the batcher scheduler thread + the actor thread both touch the connection? The `sendBatch` is called only from the batcher scheduler thread (flush). The actor thread appends to the batcher (synchronized). So `session.sendMessage` is only ever called from the batcher scheduler thread. Good — serialized.

However, there's one more subtlety: Spring's `sendMessage` **blocks**. If the client is slow/remote, the batcher scheduler thread blocks on `sendMessage`. Since the batcher scheduler is per-session (each session has its own DeltaBatcher → its own scheduler thread), a blocked send blocks only that session's flush — it does NOT block the registry actor (which only appends to the batcher, never blocks). So the actor keeps processing other sessions. That's actually BETTER than before (before, `sendMessage` was called synchronously from `endFrame` ON THE ACTOR THREAD — a slow client would block the single actor thread and stall ALL sessions!).

Wait — this is a genuinely important point. BEFORE my change: `endFrame` → `send(frame)` → `conn.send` → Spring's `session.sendMessage` **blocking on the actor thread**. A slow remote client → the single `pathland-actor` thread blocks → ALL sessions stall. So the Spring path had a worse variant of the problem (actor-thread blocking), and my change (batcher flush on a per-session scheduler thread) actually **fixes that too** — sends no longer run on the actor thread.

But — does the batching fully protect Spring? The batcher flushes every 20ms OR 16KB. With a slow client, `sendMessage` blocks the batcher scheduler thread. If it blocks long enough, the batcher's pending queue grows, and more flushes queue up on the scheduler (the scheduler is single-threaded; if the flush task blocks, subsequent scheduled flushes wait). The pending opcodes accumulate in memory (unbounded) → memory growth, but the messages are coalesced (each flush sends one big batch). Actually if the scheduler thread is blocked in sendMessage, scheduled flush tasks queue in the executor's queue — they'll run after. The batcher's `append` (on the actor) is synchronized and just adds to lists — no blocking. So the actor stays free. Memory could grow if the client is truly stuck, but the connection would eventually time out → sendMessage throws → sendBatch drops the connection → client reconnects.

- ✅ Send-failure drop → reconnect + RESYNC (shared, via sendBatch; Spring's sendMessage throws).

- ⚠️ What's NOT there for Spring: a dedicated serialized send queue (Spring's sendMessage is already synchronous/serialized — no queue needed), and no async non-blocking send. If we wanted Spring sends to be fully non-blocking, we'd need Spring's async send (`WebSocketSession.sendMessage` is blocking; there's no built-in async variant in Spring WebSocket — you'd use a `SynchronousQueue`/executor or `spring-websocket`'s `ConcurrentWebSocketSessionDecorator`).

Actually — Spring DOES offer `ConcurrentWebSocketSessionDecorator` (from `spring-websocket` / `org.springframework.web.socket.handler.ConcurrentWebSocketSessionDecorator`), which wraps a WebSocketSession to buffer messages when the session is busy sending (for messages exceeding the send-time limit, it drops or closes). That's the idiomatic Spring solution for bursts/backpressure. My `DeltaBatcher` already reduces the burst, so the decorator may be optional — but it's a robust add for Spring.

If a Spring client is slow, `sendMessage` blocks the session's batcher scheduler thread (only that session). 1. **`DeltaBatcher` coalescing** — wired into the shared `PathlandSession`, so Spring's `PathlandSocket` (→ `PathlandRegistry` → `PathlandSession`) collapses a drag burst into ~50 coalesced messages/sec just like Quarkus. No per-framework change needed.
2. **Send-failure recovery** — `sendBatch` drops the connection on failure; Spring's `session.sendMessage` **throws** on failure (it never swallowed), so a slow/overflowing Spring client → connection dropped → client reconnects + `META::RESYNC`. Spring already recovered from this; it still does.
3. **Side benefit my change added for Spring**: before, Spring's **blocking** `sendMessage` ran synchronously on the shared `pathland-actor` thread (from `endFrame`) — a slow remote client would block the single actor and stall **every session**. Now sends run on the batcher's **per-session** scheduler thread, so a slow Spring client only stalls its own session's flush.

**What Spring still lacks vs. Quarkus** (and what it doesn't need):
- The Quarkus serialized-send queue — not needed: Spring's `sendMessage` is already synchronous and internally serialized, and the batcher calls it from one thread per session.
- **Optional hardening for very slow clients**: Spring's `sendMessage` blocks; if a client stalls, its batcher thread blocks and that session's pending delta memory can grow (bounded by a reconnect, since the actor stays free). The idiomatic Spring fix is wrapping the session in `ConcurrentWebSocketSessionDecorator` (from `spring-websocket`, already on the classpath via `spring-boot-starter-websocket`) — buffers while a send is in progress and drops/closes on buffer/time limits, so extreme backpressure becomes a clean close→reconnect instead of unbounded memory.

So: bursts **are** handled for Spring today; the only optional follow-up is Spring-specific **backpressure buffering** for pathological slow clients. Want me to add the `ConcurrentWebSocketSessionDecorator` hardening to `SpringConnection` as a small follow-up on this branch?

Move the 18 assets (6 audio, 6 covers, 6 lyrics) into the shared project at
`lib/java/pathland-demo-views/src/main/resources/META-INF/resources/_pathland/assets/{audio,albumart,lyrics}/`

`META-INF/resources/` is the **standard location both web frameworks serve from dependency jars automatically**:
- **Spring Boot** default static locations include `classpath:/META-INF/resources/` (scans all jars on the classpath).
- **Quarkus** merges `META-INF/resources/` from the app + all dependency jars.

So the Quarkus and Spring demos keep serving `/_pathland/assets/...` with **zero code changes** — the demo-views jar (already a dependency of all three) now supplies them.

## Steps
1. **Move** the 18 files from the quarkus copy into `pathland-demo-views/src/main/resources/META-INF/resources/_pathland/assets/` (Maven includes `src/main/resources` in the jar automatically — no pom change).

4. **Add a regression test** in `pathland-demo-views`: assert all 18 resources resolve on the classpath (`getResourceAsStream(...) != null`), so a missing/renamed asset fails the build instead of a silent 404 in the demos.
5. **Verify**
   - `mvn -q install -DskipTests` (reactor; demo-views jar now embeds the assets).

   - `mvn test` for `pathland-demo-views` + `pathland-render-html` (its SSR test only asserts URL strings — unaffected).

## Notes / tradeoffs
- `META-INF/resources/` is chosen over a jar-root `assets/` because both web frameworks serve it from dependencies **without custom resource handlers/routes** (the alternative needs per-framework wiring for no benefit).
- The TUI demo (`pathland-tui-demo`) doesn't render media — no change.
- Net result: ~9 MB stored once instead of three times; the demos shrink accordingly.

The assets are being served extremely slow in quarkus now

The user reports: "The assets are being served extremely slow in quarkus now."

This is a regression from the asset dedup: assets moved into the `pathland-demo-views` dependency jar's `META-INF/resources/`. In Quarkus, serving static resources from a **dependency jar** is known to be slower than from the application's own `META-INF/resources` — Quarkus reads dependency-jar resources by streaming from the JAR file (opening the jar entry each request, no classpath-directory fast path), whereas app-local resources are served directly from disk.

Actually — let me think about the real mechanism. Quarkus's static resource handling: 
- App resources in `src/main/resources/META-INF/resources` are served efficiently (direct filesystem reads).
- Dependency jar resources: Quarkus supports serving `META-INF/resources` from dependencies too, but it may need to open the jar, read the entry — significantly slower, especially for large files like mp3s (~2.5-2.9 MB each). For a few MB file per request from inside a jar, that's slow (jar reads, decompression? mp3 isn't compressed in the jar unless compressed — jar entries are deflate-compressed by default; Quarkus reads via `FileSystemResource`/jar entry streaming).

So serving the mp3s from the dependency jar is slow. Also — the audio files are now ~2.5-2.9 MB each (128k mono for ~170-180s ≈ 2.6 MB), served from inside a jar. Each request streams the whole jar entry. Quarkus may also be decompressing.

Options to fix:
1. **Serve the assets from the app's own resources in each web demo** (back to duplication — defeats the dedup).

Title: Classloader optimisations for resource loading
URL: https://github.com/quarkusio/quarkus/issues/13256
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
**Description** 
This is about optimising how our (production) classloader `RunnerClassLoader` can efficiently open resources, and release the internal caches so to keep using a minimal footprint. 
 
**Implementation ideas** 
Vertx has a caching layer implemented by `io.vertx.core.file.impl.FileResolver`, which will trigger loading the full list of resources of any parent directory as well when a single resource is requested, as it attempts to then create a cache on filesystem. 
 
This is an interestin idea, but it doesn't play along well with the current implementation of the Quarkus `RunnerClassLoader`, as attempting to load e.g. `META-INF/resources/` will trigger the load on all jars which have such a resource path (which means opening many jar files). 
 
Following up on ideas discussed in #13219 , some options IMO worth considering: 
 
 - pre-load all the resources during boot, keep them in memory (and disable the Vertx FS-cache ?) 
 - actually leverage the `io.vertx.core.file.impl.FileResolver` explicitly during boot to build up the cache on filesystem, then release all caches 
 - extract the "hot resources" during build of the application into the filesystem? (For example static webpages?) 
 - we could opt to be more fine-grained indexing in the map _packages/ClassLoadingResource_ in `RunnerClassLoader`, specifically for resources to have more precision - so to hit the right jar files. 
 
## StaticResourcesBuildItem 
 
We could also take this opportunity to actually process the resources which have been explicitly mentioned by `StaticResourcesBuildItem` more optimally, and fallback to a "slow mode" (existing?) for any unlisted resource. 
 
This could be an opportunity to provide a warning about the need of a resource being loaded, as this would fail in native mode. 
 
## ServiceProviderBuildItem 
 
Similarly services from `META-INF/services/` could be specifically optimised, and we can take advantage of having a fallback mode in JVM which would produce a warning for native mode. 
 
## Testing for proper resource configuration 
 
To make it more obvious that there's a missing resource registration, I'd also propose having an environment flag which upgrades the warning into an exception. 
This would be useful during testing; although I believe it's probably best left as an opt-in to not nag people too much - especially as they might not be interested in extreme optimisations and/or native images.

Key facts:

2. **For resources inside jars, Vert.x's `FileResolverImpl` extracts them to a cache folder (`/tmp/vertx-cache`)** on first access — `unpackFromFileURL`/`unpackUrlResource`. This unpacking copies the resource out of the jar to disk. The FIRST access is slow (jar read + unpack). After that, it serves from the cache dir (fast). BUT the cache entry timeout is 30s and max-cache-size 10000 — with a `quarkus.http.static-resources.cache-entry-timeout` default of 30s, entries may be evicted and re-unpacked.
3. **Range requests** (`enable-range-support`) default `true`. For jar resources, after unpacking to disk, range works. But each range request to an mp3 might re-trigger unpacking if the cache evicted.
4. **Caching headers**: `max-age` default 24h. So Cache-Control IS set (max-age 24h) for static resources — but only when `caching-enabled` (default true). Hmm — so the browser SHOULD cache. The FileResolver unpacks to `/tmp/vertx-cache` once per resource (persisted on disk across restarts? the vertx-cache persists in the tmp dir). Actually FileResolver caches in memory + unpacks to disk once. So repeated requests should be fast after the first unpack.

The `unpackFromFileURL` path is for the FileResolver when something requests a file URL. For StaticHandler with classpath resources, it uses the classloader to get a URL and streams it — reading the jar entry per request. Whether it caches depends on the version. The `max-age` config default is 24h and `caching-enabled` default true — so dev mode SHOULD send `Cache-Control: max-age=86400` (or similar). So the browser caches. Done — the slow Quarkus asset serving is fixed, committed `758b3f7e` on `refactor/shared-demo-assets`.

## What changed
The assets stay **single-embedded** in `pathland-demo-views`, but are now served from **disk** instead of from inside the jar:

- **`DemoAssets`** (`pathland-demo-views`): `extractToTemp()` unpacks all 24 assets once at startup to `<root>/assets/…`; `GtkHost` now delegates to it (same asset-root semantics). `DemoAssetsTest` guards the 24 assets + the extraction.
- **Quarkus** (`DemoAssetsRoute`): a startup Vert.x `StaticHandler` at `/_pathland/assets/*` → the extracted dir (preempts the jar-based handler), plus `quarkus.http.static-resources.max-age=168h`.
- **Spring** (`DemoAssetsConfig`): a `WebMvcConfigurer` mapping `/_pathland/assets/**` → `file:<root>/assets/`, plus `spring.web.resources.cache.period=7d`.

## Verified (ran both apps and curled)
- **Quarkus**: track1.mp3 → `200`, `accept-ranges: bytes`, `content-length`, `cache-control: public, immutable, max-age=86400`; `Range: bytes=0-1023` → **206 Partial Content**; full 2.8 MB track in **7 ms**.
- **Spring**: same — `206` on range, full track in **5.7 ms** (vs the previous jar-based stalls on a remote host).
- `mvn -q clean install` reactor green; demo-views 16 tests + gtk-demo 6 pass.

Audio seeking now works (Range), and the browser caches media. The svg icons serve fine (no `Content-Type` from Vert.x — same as before, not a regression).

Fixed and committed `de004dc5`.

## Root cause
It wasn't a path problem — the Spring starter's `PathlandIndexController.framework` maps `/_pathland/**` (a `@Controller`, order 0) and serves `static/_pathland/<file>` from the classpath. That controller **preempted** my `DemoAssetsConfig` resource handler (which runs at lowest precedence), and since the assets had moved out of `static/_pathland/` into the demo-views jar, it returned **404**.

## What changed
- **Starter (`PathlandIndexController`)** — generalized to serve a configured **`pathland.asset-dir`** filesystem root under `/_pathland/**` (traversal-guarded), falling back after the classpath bundle lookup. Reuses its existing `Range` logic (now on a `Resource`), and adds `Cache-Control: max-age=604800, public, immutable` to the full + range responses.
- **Spring demo (`SpringDemoApplication.main`)** — sets `pathland.asset-dir` = `DemoAssets.extractToTemp()` before boot (single embedded copy, extracted once).
- **Deleted** the broken `DemoAssetsConfig` (`WebMvcConfigurer`).

- `/_pathland/assets/audio/track1.mp3` → **200**, `Content-Type: audio/mpeg`, `Content-Length`, `Accept-Ranges`, `Cache-Control`.
- `Range: bytes=0-1023` → **206** `Content-Range: bytes 0-1023/2841747`.
- `/_pathland/dom-renderer.js` still **200**; the mounted `/app2/_pathland/assets/…` also **200**.
- Full 2.8 MB track in **6 ms**.
- Reactor tests green (`mvn -q test`, excluding the two web demos).

The user asks about a reliability question: "On unstable connections important messages may be lost, and cause events or updates not to be received. Would it make sense to builtin ack for the socket transport?"

This is about the WebSocket transport between the server (Quarkus/Spring) and the DOM client (TS), and potentially the desktop path (shared-memory ring, but that's not a network socket). The user is asking whether a built-in ACK mechanism makes sense for the socket transport to handle message loss on unstable connections.

1. **The DOM client (TS) + server WebSocket**: 
   - The server sends delta frames (PLPL batches) over the WS.
   - The client applies them.
   - On connection close, the client reconnects with backoff and sends `META::RESYNC` → server re-sends a full snapshot. So there's reconnect + RESYNC recovery.
   - BUT: on a flaky connection, a message can be LOST without the connection closing (e.g., a TCP segment dropped and the WS frame silently lost? Actually TCP guarantees delivery or connection drop — a WS frame over a single TCP connection is reliable: if the TCP connection is alive, all bytes arrive. If the connection dies, TCP detects it (RST or keepalive) and the WS closes. So "message loss" on a stable-but-flaky TCP connection is rare UNLESS there's an intermediary (proxy/load balancer) that drops WS frames without closing, OR the connection is half-open (network partition where the server's TCP connection is still "open" but the client is gone, or vice versa).

   Actually — the classic problem: **half-open connections**. The server thinks the WS is open (no close frame), but the client is gone (or vice versa). Messages sent by the server are dropped (no one to receive). The client never gets them; the connection never "closes" from the client's perspective if it's the SERVER that's partitioned... wait. Let me think.

   The scenario the user describes: "On unstable connections important messages may be lost, and cause events or updates not to be received." So the server sends updates; some are lost; the client misses them and never knows.

   Cases:
   a. **Server→client message loss without close**: if a proxy drops a WS frame mid-stream or the TCP connection is half-open (server's send fails silently — which we FIXED for Quarkus by closing the connection on send failure). With the Quarkus fix, a failed send → connection closed → client reconnects + RESYNC. So partial loss is mostly handled by reconnect+RESYNC IF the failure is detected. But a silently-dropped frame (no error surfaced) is undetectable without ACKs.

   b. **Client→server message loss**: e.g., the client's VALUE_CHANGED event is lost → the server never processes it → the app state misses the update. The client doesn't know. This is the "events not received" part.

   c. **Out-of-order or duplicate delivery**: TCP guarantees ordering on a single connection; but proxies/reconnects could reorder (a stale WS from a previous connection delivering after a reconnect? The WS is one connection; a reconnect creates a new one). Duplicates possible on reconnect (a RESYNC snapshot + a delta that was also sent).

2. **Current reliability mechanisms**:
   - **Reconnect + RESYNC**: on WS close, the client reconnects with exponential backoff and sends `META::RESYNC` → server re-sends the full tree snapshot. This recovers from detected connection loss. `frameCount` in the header — the client tracks frames? Let me check. The client sends RESYNC on reconnect (`st()`). The server's `resync()` → `renderFull` → full snapshot.
   - **Delta batching** (the DeltaBatcher) reduces message count.
   - **Quarkus send failure → close** (just fixed): converts silent-stall into reconnect+RESYNC.

3. **What an ACK mechanism would add**:
   - **Client→server ACKs with a sequence number**: the server tags each batch with a monotonically increasing `frameCount` (already in the PLPL header — `frameCount` field!). The client ACKs the highest contiguous `frameCount` received. The server keeps an unacked buffer; if the client doesn't ACK within a window, the server knows a message was lost and either (a) re-sends the unacked delta(s), or (b) triggers a RESYNC.
   - **Server→client ACKs for client events**: the client sends events; if an important event (e.g., VALUE_CHANGED) must not be lost, the client needs an ACK and a retry. But most input events are idempotent-ish (a slider value set twice = same result); losing a VALUE_CHANGED just means the server keeps the older value — the next change fixes it. Text input: losing a TEXT_CHANGED means the server text is stale — the client could resend on the next change. For events, an ACK + retransmit buffer is heavier.

Let me think about what's actually valuable and proportionate:

**The core insight**: The protocol already has `frameCount` (u32) in every PLPL batch header (both directions). And there's `META::RESYNC` for full recovery. The gap is **gap detection without a full reconnect**.

**A proportional design:**
1. **Client→server ACK**: the client periodically (or on each batch) reports the highest contiguous `frameCount` it has applied, as a lightweight host→guest message (e.g., a `META` opcode or a small event). The server tracks per-session `ackFrameCount`. If the server sends a delta with `frameCount = N` and the client's ACK stays below N for too long (or the client's next message indicates a gap), the server can **re-send from the last-acked point** (replay buffered deltas) OR just issue a **RESYNC** (full snapshot — simpler, already implemented).

2. **Server→client gap detection**: since the server is the one that knows what it sent, if the client reports a gap (its ack < the frames it should have), the server resends or resyncs.

3. **Client→server event reliability**: for important events, the client could retry or the server could ACK. But given most events are idempotent (value/text), the simplest is: the client tracks unacknowledged events and on reconnect resends them; OR rely on the fact that the server's state is the source of truth and a missed event is corrected by the next interaction or a RESYNC.

**Actually — the SIMPLEST and most robust approach given the existing design**: 
- **ACK-based gap detection that triggers RESYNC**. The server doesn't need to buffer/replay deltas (complex, memory). Instead:
  - The client ACKs the highest contiguous `frameCount` (piggybacked on its next outbound message, or a periodic ping-ish ack).
  - The server, on receiving an ACK that reveals a gap (client missed frames), initiates a `META::RESYNC` (server→client) — full snapshot recovery. OR the client, on detecting its own gap (a frame arrives out of sequence / a gap in frameCount), requests RESYNC itself.
- This is "built-in ack for the socket transport" in a pragmatic form: **sequence-based gap detection + RESYNC**, no replay buffer.

## Summary

On unstable connections, important messages can be lost **silently** and never be received:

- **Server → client deltas**: on a half-open/silently-broken connection (NAT/keepalive drop, proxy frame loss, dead peer) the server keeps sending into a socket that "looks" open; no close is detected, so the existing reconnect + `META::RESYNC` recovery never fires → stale UI.
- **Client → server events**: browser `send()` is optimistic, so an important `VALUE_CHANGED`/`TEXT_CHANGED` sent into a broken connection is dropped and **neither side notices** → stale app state.

TCP already guarantees ordering/no-loss on a genuinely live connection, and detected drops already recover via reconnect + `META::RESYNC`. The gap is **undetectable** loss (half-open) and **client→server event** loss. The fix is a lightweight, sequence-based **built-in ACK** that makes delivery observable and drives the existing recovery paths.

## Design

**Protocol (spec-first):**
- New `META::ACK = 0x04` (both directions; `spec/OPCODE.md` + `pathland-core` constant + `Commands.Meta.ACK` + a `spec/CONFORMANCE.md` golden vector). Field `A` = the highest contiguous sequence counter of the **peer's** stream this side processed.
  - client→server: ACKs server frame batches (recovery + liveness).
  - server→client: ACKs the client's event sequence (lets the client drop its retransmit buffer; doubles as the heartbeat).
- Sequencing contract (network-batch section): every server→client batch carries a per-session monotonic `frameCount` (field exists today — Java server sends 0); every client→server event batch carries a per-connection monotonic event sequence.

**Server (`pathland-server-core`):**
- Stamp each flushed batch with an incrementing `frameCount`.
- **Bounded replay buffer** (~last 64 frames / ~256 KB) of sent batches; evicted as the client ACKs. On an ACK **gap** → replay `ack+1..lastSent` in order; beyond the buffer → server-driven `META::RESYNC` fallback.
- **Liveness**: per-session `lastClientActivity`; no ACK/message within ~30 s → drop the connection (client reconnects + RESYNC). Keep the existing Quarkus send-failure-close.
- **Event ACK**: track the last processed client event sequence; emit `META::ACK` (server→client) in the next batch + a periodic idle heartbeat.

**Client (`lib/typescript`):**
- Track the highest **contiguous applied** `frameCount`; send throttled `META::ACK` (~250 ms) + idle heartbeat.
- Stamp outbound event batches with an event sequence; **buffer unacked events** (latest-per-control, bounded); drop acked on the server ACK; **resend unacked on reconnect** (events are idempotent).
- **Read-timeout liveness**: no server message within ~15–30 s → close → reconnect + RESYNC (catches a dead server client-side too).

## Notes
- No per-message retransmission of server deltas beyond the bounded replay buffer; reconnect+RESYNC stays the ultimate recovery.
- Replayed frames are safe: TCP ordering means the client never applies anything beyond its ack, so replay delivers exactly the missing frames; reconnect is deduped by RESYNC.
- `status.md` updates for `pathland-core`, `pathland-server-core`, `lib/typescript`.

## Verification
Rust conformance vector; Java tests (batcher sequencing, replay-on-gap, buffer-overflow→RESYNC, ack-timeout close, server→client ACK); TS tests (applied-frameCount tracking, throttled ACK, reconnect resends unacked events, read-timeout); live flaky-link check against the Quarkus demo.

Related: #114 (Quarkus send-failure-close), #115 (delta batching).
